original_value: The aim of this article is to investigate the impact of data breach severity on the readability of mandatory data breach notification letters. Using a content analysis approach to determine data breach severity attributes (measured by the total number of breached records, type of data accessed, the source of the data breach, and how the data were used), in conjunction with readability measures (reading complexity, numerical intensity, length of letter, word size, and unique words), 512 data breach incidents from 281 U.S. firms across the 2012–2015 period were examined. The results indicate that data breach severity has a positive impact on reading complexity, length of letter, word size, and unique words, and a negative impact on numerical terms. Interpreting the results collectively through the lens of impression management, it can be inferred that business managers may be attempting to obfuscate bad news associated with high data breach severity incidents by manipulating syntactical features of the data breach notification letters in a way that makes the message difficult for individuals to comprehend. The study contributes to the information studies and impression management behavior literatures by analyzing linguistic cues in notifications following a data breach incident.

result.paraphrase: This article examines how data breach severity affects the readability of mandatory breach notification letters. Using content analysis to assess severity attributes—measured by the total number of records breached, the type of data accessed, the source of the breach, and how the data were used—alongside readability metrics such as reading complexity, numerical intensity, letter length, word size, and unique words, the study analyzed 512 breach incidents from 281 U.S. firms over 2012–2015. The findings show that greater breach severity increases reading complexity, letter length, word size, and unique words, while reducing numerical terms. Taken together and viewed through impression management theory, the results suggest that managers may try to obscure bad news tied to severe breach incidents by altering the syntactic features of notification letters to make them harder to understand. The study adds to the information studies and impression management behavior literatures by examining linguistic cues in post-breach notifications.
